mcqs.question: Before generics, an `Object`-based container required a cast to retrieve elements. What did generics change about when a type mismatch on that container surfaces?
options: Type mismatches now surface only at the moment the program is compiled, never at runtime
Nothing changed — mismatches still only surface at the pop/read site via ClassCastException
Generic containers eliminate the need for any type checking at all
The mismatch is caught at the mismatched push/insert site as a compile error, instead of surfacing later as a runtime ClassCastException at the read site
mcqs.explanation: Generics move the point of failure earlier: a wrongly-typed insertion into a Stack<String> is now a compile error where the bad push happens, rather than a runtime cast failure that could surface far away at the read site. Runtime errors from other causes still exist, so it's not purely compile-time, and generics don't eliminate type checking — they make it stricter, not absent.

mcqs.question: Under type erasure, what is true about `Box<Int>` and `Box<String>` at runtime?
options: They share the identical compiled method bodies, with T replaced by Object/Any, and the compiler inserts casts at the boundaries to preserve the appearance of type safety
They are compiled into two entirely separate classes with distinct machine code, exactly as monomorphization would produce
Box<Int> is compiled but Box<String> is rejected at compile time
Neither type actually exists at runtime; both are removed entirely by the compiler
mcqs.explanation: Erasure means one shared compiled implementation serves every instantiation, with casts inserted at read boundaries — this is the defining difference from monomorphization's separate specialized copies. Both instantiations do exist and run at runtime; erasure doesn't remove the class entirely, it removes only the generic type parameter's runtime representation.

mcqs.question: Rust's monomorphization generates a separate compiled copy of a generic function for each concrete type it's used with. What is the direct consequence of this?
options: Rust programs cannot use generics with more than one concrete type in the same binary
Compiled binary size and compile time grow with the number of distinct type instantiations, in exchange for each instantiation being as optimized as hand-written type-specific code
Monomorphization makes Rust's generics slower than Java's erased generics at runtime
Monomorphization eliminates the need for type bounds on generic parameters
mcqs.explanation: Generating a specialized copy per instantiation is exactly what trades increased binary size and compile time for per-type runtime optimization — the core cost/benefit of monomorphization. Rust freely supports many instantiations in one binary, monomorphized code is generally faster than erased code at runtime (not slower), and bounds are still needed to constrain what operations a generic body can perform.

mcqs.question: Why can't you write `new T[10]` directly inside a generic Java class, forcing developers toward the `(T[]) new Object[10]` workaround?
options: Because Java arrays cannot hold any generic type under any circumstances
Because array creation always requires a no-argument constructor, which generic types don't have
Because the workaround produces an array with no supported operations at all
Because arrays retain their element type at runtime, but T has already been erased by the time the array would need to be created, leaving no concrete type for the JVM to give the array
mcqs.explanation: Arrays are reified (they know their element type at runtime) while generics are erased, so there's a genuine mismatch: creating a T[] would need a concrete type that erasure has already discarded, hence the restriction. Arrays of generic-adjacent types are used all the time via workarounds, array creation has nothing to do with no-arg constructors, and the workaround array is fully usable, just misleadingly typed underneath.

mcqs.question: What does Go's generics implementation (1.18+) do differently from a strict erasure-vs-monomorphization binary choice?
options: It always fully erases every generic type, identical to Java
It always fully monomorphizes every generic instantiation, identical to Rust
It disallows generics from being used with more than two concrete types per function
It groups types with identical machine representations into shared implementations while specializing where representations genuinely differ, landing between full erasure and full monomorphization
mcqs.explanation: Go's hybrid approach — partial specialization based on shared representations — deliberately avoids being purely one extreme, unlike Java's full erasure or Rust's full monomorphization. It is not identical to either language's approach, and there's no such two-instantiation limit on Go generics.
